metadata.description: Does the learner know that thawing happens cold and takes planning?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A big cut thaws safely in the refrigerator because the whole piece stays cold the entire time. It takes days for a large shoulder, so starting early matters. If you run short on time, a cold-water bath with the water changed often is the other safe way.
On the counter, the outside warms into the temperature range where bacteria multiply quickly while the middle is still frozen. Thaw in the refrigerator instead, and start several days ahead.
Warm water brings the outside of the meat into the danger zone long before the center thaws. If you need a faster method, use cold water in a sealed bag and change the water regularly.

A frozen center takes a very long time to warm up in a low-temperature cooker, while the surface sits in the danger zone. Plan ahead and thaw the meat completely, in the refrigerator, before it goes on.

metadata.description: Does the learner know the standard probe position?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: The thickest part is the last place to come up to temperature, so that reading tells you the whole piece is there. Keeping the tip off the bone matters because bone can read hotter or cooler than the meat around it.
Bone conducts heat differently from meat and can give a false reading. Keep the tip in the meat, in the thickest part, clear of bone.
The surface heats first, so a shallow reading runs well ahead of the center. Push the tip into the thickest part of the cut.
The side nearest the fire is the part that is ahead, so it tells you the least about the slowest part. Check the thickest part, where the meat lags.

metadata.description: Does the learner go beyond one reading when the cut is uneven?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Large or irregular cuts have cooler pockets, and a single reading can miss them. Several readings with the coolest one counting gives you a more honest picture, which matters most for safety.
This is the standard habit and usually works. On an uneven or very large cut one reading can miss a cooler pocket, so it is a good start rather than the full check.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: sound single-point practice, but the question asks for the most reliable approach on a thick, uneven cut.

connections.feedback: Bone can read hotter or cooler than the meat beside it, so a reading against bone does not describe the meat. Keep the tip in meat, clear of bone.
The fire side is the part that is ahead, so it hides the slowest part of the cut. Read where the meat lags, not where it leads.

metadata.description: Does the learner treat thick white smoke as a fire problem, not a flavor bonus?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Thick white smoke usually means the fire is starved of air and smoldering, and that smoke can taste harsh and bitter on the meat. More air lets the wood burn cleanly, and the smoke thins to a pale, almost blue wisp. Load the meat when it does.
Heavy white smoke is not more flavor. It tends to deposit a harsh, bitter coating on the meat. Wait for thin, pale smoke before loading.
Choking the air supply is what makes a fire smolder and smoke heavily. Do the opposite: give the fire more air so the wood burns cleaner.
Wet wood adds steam and cools the fire, so it tends to smolder more, not less. The fix is airflow and a hot, established fire.

sets.label: basic / backyard host for a crowd / leftovers

metadata.description: Does the host know the two-hour rule and quick cooling?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Bacteria multiply quickly in the danger zone, so cooked food should not sit out longer than about two hours. Setting a timer when the food comes off helps.
A shallow layer cools much faster than a deep pot, so the middle spends less time in the danger zone. Split big batches before chilling.
Waiting for steam to stop can eat the whole safe window, and a deep pan stays warm in the middle for hours. Portion into shallow containers and refrigerate promptly.
Light home smoking does not make cooked meat safe to leave out. Smoked meat is held to the same time limits as any other cooked food.

sets.label: intermediate / home enthusiast / stall hour six

metadata.description: Does the learner recognise a stall as normal and know the common choices?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A pause like this is normal. Moisture evaporating from the surface cools the meat about as fast as the cooker heats it, so the number sits still for a while. Steady heat gets you through it without risking the cook.

Wrapping traps moisture and usually shortens the stall. Foil is the fastest and softens the bark, while butcher paper breathes and keeps more of it. Both are accepted methods and the right pick depends on your schedule and the bark you want.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: wrapping is a widely used, legitimate technique with a bark trade-off. Not wrong, but not the only sound answer.

connections.feedback: A moderate increase can shorten the stall, and many cooks do it when time is tight. The trade-off is a faster, drier finish and less margin for error, so it suits a recipe you know well.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: hot-and-faster is a real school of thought with a texture trade-off.

connections.feedback: Each peek lets heat and smoke escape and lengthens the cook, which is the opposite of what you want. Trust the probe and leave the lid down.

metadata.description: Does the learner keep a charcoal fire outdoors and clear of buildings?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Burning charcoal makes carbon monoxide, which you cannot see or smell and which can build up fast in a covered space. Run the cooker outside in the open, clear of buildings and anything that can catch fire. A little rain is the lesser problem.
An open garage door does not move enough air to be safe, and carbon monoxide can drift into the house. Charcoal cookers belong outdoors, in the open.
A roof traps heat and fumes, and an attached porch lets carbon monoxide drift indoors. Heat and sparks can also damage the structure. Move out into the open.
Heat, sparks and flare-ups can ignite siding and eaves, and fumes can find their way inside. Keep the cooker well clear of the house.

sets.label: intermediate / backyard host for a crowd / holding brisket

metadata.description: Does the host know how to hold finished meat safely?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A wrapped brisket in a preheated insulated cooler stays hot and moist for hours. Keep it above the safe hot-holding temperature, and check it with a thermometer when you are unsure.
Left out, the brisket cools into the danger zone within a short time, and the surface dries out. Hold it hot in an insulated cooler or a low oven.

Chilling and reheating is safe if the cooling is quick and the reheating is thorough, and caterers rely on it. You usually lose some texture and juiciness compared with a hot hold, so it suits cases where you cannot hold hot.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: a legitimate safe method with a quality trade-off, not the best fit for a four-hour wait.

connections.feedback: Four more hours at cooking temperature will dry the meat out and turn the bark leathery. Hold it hot at a lower temperature, wrapped, instead.

metadata.description: Does the learner judge chicken by temperature and not color or time?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: For poultry, the safe minimum is the line that matters, and every extra degree dries out lean breast meat. Check the thickest part, away from bone, and take it off when it gets there.
Color and clear juices are not reliable signs that poultry is safe. Use a thermometer in the thickest part.
Skin color depends on sugar in the rub and on the cooker, and tells you nothing about the inside. Check the temperature instead.
Cook times vary with the cooker, the weather and the size of the pieces. A recipe time says when to start checking, not when to stop.

metadata.description: Does the learner understand that safe is not the same as tender?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A shoulder is safe long before it is tender. The tough connective tissue needs time and heat to soften, and the probe sliding in with little resistance tells you that has happened. Use the number to know when to start checking.
Many cooks use a number in the low 200s as the signal to start probing, and it often lines up with tender meat. Pieces vary, so the feel of the probe is the deciding check.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: a target number is a useful guide, but it should be confirmed by feel.

connections.feedback: Bark color depends on sugar, spice and the fire, not on whether the connective tissue has softened. A dark shoulder can still be tough inside. Probe it.
The safe minimum is far below the temperature at which a shoulder turns tender, so pulling it there gives you a tough, chewy result. Safe is not the same as done for a pulled cut.
